title: Concepts Worth Having: Refining VLM-Guided Concept Bottleneck Models with Minimal Annotations
claim: Prior concept models trust noisy VLM-derived labels; ours propagates a few expert annotations through the embedding space to correct them.
layout: 2 stacked panels, left-to-right flow, ours adds a GP heatmap module
description: Two stacked rows, each a left-to-right pipeline on a light gray background. The top row, VLM-CBM, takes a face photo through a VLM icon, which is fed by a Vocabulary box. It produces concept activations such as "Is blonde?: Yes", marked with a red cross, and "Wears makeup?: Yes", marked with a green check. These feed a Linear g box and the output "woman". The bottom row, VH-CBM, uses the same photo, VLM and vocabulary. It adds an Expert icon and a stack of per-concept Gaussian Process panels. These are blue-and-red contour maps with dotted arrows from the expert's labeled points, and the VLM embedding z lands as a point on the map. The row outputs concept statistics μ and σ, now with "Is blonde?: No" and a green check, then Linear g and "woman". The red error mark against green checks shows the contrast, and the colorful GP map draws the eye.
caption: Top: VLM-CBMs rely solely on concepts provided by VLMs -- either at inference time (as above) or for distilling a concept extractor $g$, cf. [ref] -- which can be inaccurate, compromising interpretability [ref]. Bottom: \method exploits the VLM's embedding space to propagate expert concept supervision to obtain concept statistics (i.e., $\vmu$ and $\vsigma$ from the GP) for any test point, improving concept accuracy with few annotations.
abstract: Concept-bottleneck models (CBMs) are neural classifiers that compute predictions from high-level concepts extracted from the input. CBMs ensure stakeholders can understand the concepts -- and the predictions they entail -- by learning these from concept-level annotations, which are however seldom available. Recent CBM architectures work around this issue by obtaining annotations from Vision-Language Models (VLMs). While greatly broadening applicability, doing so can yield lower quality concepts and therefore less interpretable models. We strike for a middle ground by introducing Vision-plus-Human-guided CBM (VH-CBM), a hybrid approach that exploits both VLMs and a small amount of dense annotations. VH-CBM employs a Gaussian Process in the VLM's embedding space, which captures useful global information about the target domain, to propagate the expert's supervision to any target data point. Our empirical evaluation shows how VH-CBM predicts more accurate concepts than VLM-guided CBMs even when annotating as little as 1% of the data, while sporting better concept calibration and supporting active learning.
